uncited: *   **Input:** A volumetric dataset defined on a BCC lattice, camera parameters (view and projection matrices), and a rendering kernel (typically Gaussian or similar spherical filter).
The data is stored in a BCC lattice structure.
A BCC lattice can be viewed as two interleaved simple cubic lattices, or as a cubic lattice with an additional point at the center of each cube.
*   **Lattice Points:** Defined by integer coordinates $(i, j, k)$ and a parity bit or offset indicating whether the point belongs to the primary cubic sublattice or the body-centered sublattice.
*   **Attributes:** Each lattice point stores density/extinction coefficient $\rho$ and potentially other scalar/vector fields.
**Lattice Generation:** Construct the BCC grid from the input data.
If the input is on a CC grid, resample or interpolate onto the BCC lattice.
**Slicing/Sorting:** Sort the transformed points by depth (Z-buffer) to ensure correct front-to-back or back-to-front compositing.
**Rasterization (Splatting):** For each point, project its 3D footprint onto the 2D image plane.
This ensures that the sampling pattern aligns correctly with the screen pixels during rasterization.
**Compositing:** Accumulate the splatted contributions into the frame buffer using alpha blending.
*   **Time Complexity:** Rendering time is proportional to the number of sample points.
Requires careful handling of the 1/2 shift during rasterization.
*   **When to Use:** Point-based volume rendering of isotropic data where memory and performance are critical.
*   **When Not to Use:** Non-isotropic signals, or when compatibility with standard CC-based tools is required.
The BCC grid was introduced as an alternative to the Cubic Cartesian (CC) grid for volumetric data representation.
